Author: Norris, Debra Hess; Kennedy, Nora W.; Lavédrine, Bertrand
Title: INTRODUCTION
Abstract: Conservation of Photographs: Significance, Use and Care provides an overview of theory, research and practice in the preservation of photographic collections - from the early daguerreotype to the arrival of contemporary digital prints - held in museums, historic sites, libraries, archives and communities globally. It is certainly difficult to share a common definition of a photograph today, given the many technological changes undergone since its introduction, and in particular the development of digital techniques. Each of the editors of this book may have a different idea of what a photograph is, but we all share a concern for its conservation and dissemination. Therefore, the interest arose to bring together a body of knowledge serving as an important practical reference for photograph conservators and an essential resource for emerging practitioners. Conservation of Photographs is a tribute to the value and significance of photography and the impact of this remarkable medium worldwide. Written by nearly 100 leading international professionals, this book is a labor of their love and commitment, and a tribute to the synergistic advancements in photograph conservation in recent decades. Connecting material, imaging, computational and natural sciences, aesthetics, ethics and philosophy, history, art history, art and cultural context studies, these engaging writings contextualize our photographic heritage and its long-term preservation - past, present and future. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Debra Hess Norris, Nora W. Kennedy and Bertrand Lavédrine; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Magnin, Emilie
Title: Brandie Macdonald: Conserving “Us”: Caring for living heritage, oral tradition, and Indigenous knowledge
Abstract: What does it take to care for living heritage and Indigenous knowledge? What does it mean to conserve oral tradition or spiritual performance? Brandie Macdonald, Executive Director at the Indiana University Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology and former Senior Director of Decolonizing Initiatives at the Museum of Us in San Diego, discusses these and related questions in the light of her work at the Museum of Us. Among the issues raised are how Indigenous performance might be preserved in and beyond institutions, what decolonization might mean in an institution concerned with Indigenous culture, what intellectual property means in these contexts, how museums can become spaces for engaging with living objects, and how to approach these through a decolonized lens. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Hanna B. Hölling, Jules Pelta Feldman, and Emilie Magnin; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Bancroft, Anne; Fifi, Daniela
Title: Not in My Name: Heritage Conservation, Collection Care, and Repatriation within Caribbean Collections
Abstract: This chapter delves into the critical issues surrounding the care of Caribbean collections and explores repatriation and decolonisation through tangible, moveable objects, but alongside the intangible and immoveable. The Caribbean region has a diverse cultural heritage, encompassing the Indigenous, colonial, and post-colonial, embodied in a myriad of objects, including natural specimens, human remains, archaeological artefacts, artwork, decorative arts, and historical documents. These invaluable cultural assets dispersed in museums, cultural institutions, and private collections have typically originated from previous colonial spaces, leading to complex debates regarding capacities, rightful ownership, physical and intellectual authority, and preservation and conservation methodologies. A key trope against repatriation is the need for improved facilities and conservation expertise within the communities of origin. This chapter references the historical context of the Caribbean’s colonial past, underpinned by the legacy of enslavement, issues of displacement, and the consequential removal of artefacts, resources, and authority from the Caribbean region. It speaks to the colonial edict and the anthropological lens through which the “other” defined and interpreted the Caribbean (meaning the foreign, absentee, and governing minority). It examines how this historical inheritance has shaped contentious issues of provenance, rightful ownership, and governance as various island nations seek repatriation and reparations of their tangible and intangible cultural heritage. In short, it explores how Caribbean people are reclaiming their cultural authority. This chapter enters repatriation framed through an ideological standpoint in curatorial discourse as well as through conventional modes of returning objects to their communities of origin. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Daniela Fifi; individual chapters, the contributors.
Manual Tags: Heritage conservation; Cultural institutions; Cultural heritages; Historic preservation; Human remains; Archaeological artifacts; Critical issues; Cultural assets; Decorative arts; Historical documents; Rightful ownership

Author: Hölling, Hanna; Feldman, Jules Pelta; Magnin, Emilie
Title: Performance: The Ethics and the Politics of Conservation and Care, Volume II
Abstract: Representing the output of the research project “Performance: Conservation, Materiality, Knowledge,” this volume brings together diverse voices, methods, and formats in the discussion and practice of performance conservation. Conservators, artists, curators and scholars explore the ontology of performance art through its creation and institutionalization into an astonishing range of methods and approaches for keeping performance alive and well, whether inside museum collections or through folk traditions. Anchored in the disciplines of contemporary art conservation, art history, and performance studies, the contributions range far beyond these to include perspectives from anthropology, musicology, dance, law, heritage studies, and other fields. While its focus is on performance as understood in the context of contemporary art, the book’s notion of performance is much wider, including other media such as music, theater, and dance as well as an open-ended concept of performance as a vital force across culture(s). While providing cutting-edge research on an emerging and important topic, this volume remains accessible to all interested readers, allowing it to serve as a singularly valuable resource for museum professionals, scholars, students, and practitioners. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Hanna B. Hölling, Jules Pelta Feldman, and Emilie Magnin; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Hölling, Hanna; Feldman, Jules Pelta; Magnin, Emilie
Title: Introduction: Sustaining care for performance
Abstract: This introduction opens the anthology Performance: The Ethics and the Politics of Conservation and Care, volume II. The book builds upon the groundwork laid by its predecessor, volume I, which explored the intersection of performance, conservation, and care. Resulting from an interdisciplinary research project, “Performance: Conservation, Materiality, Knowledge,” both books take a deep dive into the complexities of preserving performance-based art, challenging conventional conservation norms and expanding the horizons of what can be conserved. Volume II continues this exploration, offering perspectives from various geographical, thematic, and philosophical angles. It explores ritual, music, community traditions, contemporary museum practices, and experimental art forms, presenting an innovative methodology for comprehending the potential of performance conservation within the domains of art, museums, and beyond. At the heart of this volume’s introduction lies the concept of ‘care ethics,' which underscores both the pragmatic and emotional facets of care. Drawing inspiration from feminist care theorists like Virginia Held, Eva Feder Kittay, and Joan C. Tronto, the authors scrutinize care as a fundamental moral framework underpinning human interdependence and relationships with the world, and as a notion that stretches beyond artworks themselves to encompass living bodies, artists, performers, and communities. The introduction spotlights the disparities within the art world, where issues like low wages and the exploitation of museum staff are rampant. It calls for a comprehensive understanding of care that values and supports the labor of all museum stakeholders. The concept of ‘shared guardianship’ is explored as museums collaborate with external groups and individuals to care for their collections, nurturing diverse perspectives and expertise. The text also acknowledges the political dimension of care, as the selection of works for preservation involves choices that can either be inclusive or exclusive. It underscores the challenges faced by works from marginalized groups and those resistant to dominant art-historical narratives, highlighting that loss often occurs due to discrimination within historicization. The authors challenge the dominance of Western-centric perspectives in conservation and museum practices, advocating for a more inclusive and holistic approach to care that transcends binaries and embraces the responsibilities of care in human-decentered cosmologies. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Hanna B. Hölling, Jules Pelta Feldman, and Emilie Magnin; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Magnin, Emilie
Title: Performance in the museum: Shifting roles in performance art stewardship
Abstract: This chapter explores how live performance escapes the traditional museum’s temporality of storage and exhibition and resists the standard processes of musealization. It argues that performance ultimately calls for alternative models of care and stewardship. Case studies point toward new collective ways of owning and caring, but also underline the difficulties that hinder essential changes. Finally, to suggest how performance could be collectively cared for and could endure differently, this chapter will present the idea of mycelium as a distributed, resilient, and living system that survives and expands in various ways-much like performance itself. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Hanna B. Hölling, Jules Pelta Feldman, and Emilie Magnin; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Veldpaus, Loes; Szemző, Hanna
Title: HERITAGE AS A MATTER OF CARE, AND CONSERVATION AS CARING FOR THE MATTER
Abstract: In this chapter we explore how care, as a concept, can help create new perspectives on our relations with the historic environment, and more specifically practices of adaptive reuse of built heritage. We argue that using the concept of ‘care’ instead of ‘protection’ as a frame for how we approach and deal with heritage can change how we conceptualize and undertake conservation as a practice. We illustrate our thinking through two case studies: High Street West, Sunderland (United Kingdom) and Hof Prädikow in Prädikow near Berlin (Germany). By conceptually (re)framing heritage as what María Puig de la Bellacasa calls a ‘matter of care, ' and conservation practices as the ways we care about, for, or through heritage, we explore how an ethics of care perspective can help to rethink the ways we deal with our built heritage. © 2022 selection and editorial matter, Angelika Gabauer, Sabine Knierbein, Nir Cohen, Henrik Lebuhn, Kim Trogal, Tihomir Viderman, and Tigran Haas; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Boersma, Susanne; Tietmeyer, Elisabeth
Title: Ethical practices in participatory memory work: Examples from the Museum Europäischer Kulturen in Berlin
Abstract: Ethics in museums often sit at the heart of discussions about collecting practices and questions of repatriation, yet their role in other museum practices rarely gains attention in the field. International and national codes of ethics have recently begun to be revised to ensure that they reflect the social responsibility of museums, such as through guidelines on the relational aspect of (participatory) museum work. Recent studies point to the relevance of ethics in participatory museum work without clearly describing the practical application of (old or revised) ethical principles. Equally, museum practitioners rarely prioritise ethics in their day-to-day work. However, as museums increasingly apply participatory approaches, their staff should consider the different ethical practices that require their attention, amongst which are accessibility, truthful representation, positionality, and care. This chapter provides a basis for the work that is yet to be done to ensure ethical practices for all those involved and proposes a participatory approach to defining the ethical considerations for a project. In this chapter, we discuss different codes of conduct and assess how these shape the practices that are part of participatory projects today. Rather than further theorising ethics, we build on practical examples from different participatory projects. From participation as a necessary means to truthful representation to consent forms as integral to the practice of care, the examples drawn from the work of the Museum Europäischer Kulturen - Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, Stiftung Preußischer Kulturbesitz highlight different tools and procedures that ensure ethical practices in museums. In doing so, this practice-based chapter points to processes of learning and discusses how ethical codes and practices can be tailored to support the museum’s participatory work in the future. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Gertraud Koch and Rachel Charlotte Smith; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Norris, Debra Hess; Brown, Heather; Cunningham-Kruppa, Ellen; Price, Lee; Lim, Cheralyn; Kehoe, Amber; Pénichon, Sylvie; Brogdon-Grantham, Shannon A.; Vasallos, Ioannis; Celma, Marta García; Norris, Robert; Hage-Felder, Heba
Title: PRACTICING ADVOCACY, ADVANCING STRATEGIC PRESERVATION, AND DEVELOPING OUTREACH INITIATIVES
Abstract: While much of this book describes the work of photograph conservators, this chapter addresses the broader audience of photograph collection caretakers: conservators, collection managers, archivists, librarians, and any other professionals or community members responsible for the care and preservation of photographic holdings. Caretakers do not operate in isolation. Rather, they connect with decision makers, allied professionals, and communities simultaneously to promote the care of our photographic heritage. By working together, these collections will be revealed, documented, and preserved. Aiming to advance the worth and meaning of photograph and image collections worldwide, photograph caretakers can help to imagine and initiate a range of educational partnerships and preservation projects. As advocates for photograph preservation, caretakers work with others to build visibility through marketing and social media, establish practical short-and long-term implementation plans, communicate effectively, promote respect, harness passion and creativity, and take risks. Through active listening, strategic leadership, advocacy, collaboration, and community engagement, the practice of photograph preservation and conservation can cross boundaries, build trust, and bridge divides. Strategies introduced in this chapter aim to strengthen and enrich this essential work, and to inspire you to practice advocacy and pursue strategic outreach initiatives of your own. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Debra Hess Norris, Nora W. Kennedy and Bertrand Lavédrine; individual chapters, the contributors.
Manual Tags: Decision making; Social media; Active listening; Decision makers; Educational partnerships; Image collections; Marketing media; Preservation project; Strategic collaboration; Strategic communities; Strategic leadership

Author: Jenkins, Samantha
Title: Problem Plastics at the People’s History Museum
Abstract: Plastic-based objects have become increasingly common over the last 50 years, and inevitably museums must collect plastic objects if they are to represent contemporary society. Many of these plastics, however, are inherently unstable and will deteriorate at an accelerated rate, even with strong conservation care. How, then, can museums balance the need to represent the world around them, with ensuring the safety of the objects in their collection, and the knowledge that plastic materials will eventually degrade too far for use? Using a case study at People’s History Museum, this paper looks at how museums can approach collecting contemporary plastic objects to balance the desire to collect with the reality of resourcing requirements and availability in the museum sector. People’s History Museum has been able to build a strong foundation for these decisions by creating an assessment matrix, a dedicated policy for collecting plastics and an in-depth procedure for both acquisition assessment and continuing care. While the decisions were made based on plastic materials, these also heralded a change in attitude towards collections and deaccessioning overall, necessitating a rethink of what it means to hold objects ‘in perpetuity’, and considering what the base reasons for collecting any object truly is. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Jen Kavanagh, Ellie Miles, Rosamund Lily West with Susanna Cordner; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Fifi, Daniela
Title: Forging Community and Cultural Identity during a Pandemic: Collection Digitisation in Haiti and Barbados
Abstract: The spread of the SARS-CoV-2 virus was an unexpected crisis for countries worldwide. Museums faced many challenges, including closures, funding shortages, cutting staff, and care for their collections. Digitisation proposed a viable means of providing access to programming, collection preservation, and community engagement. This chapter examines the various ways Caribbean museums overcame hurdles through the pandemic, which is argued to be an ongoing challenge for many museums today. It will explore the various digitisation efforts that enhanced collection preservation, repatriation efforts, community dialogue, and cultural identity building. Case studies of Musée Ogier-Fombrun in Haiti and the Barbados Mercury Gazette at the Barbados Archives will be examined, and the theoretical framing of Stuart Hall will be reviewed for cultural identity considerations. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Daniela Fifi; individual chapters, the contributors.
Manual Tags: Digitisation; Cultural identity; Case-studies; Fundings; Community engagement; Community dialogues; Community identities

Author: Kane, Natalie; Gardner, Corinna; Park, Juhee
Title: Social media enters the museum: Collecting WeChat at the Victoria and Albert Museum
Abstract: This chapter examines approaches to digital collecting that prioritize an understanding of design and its interconnection to society at the Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) in London. The V&A curators’ commitment to capturing design experience and its associated network of use and influence, alongside the digital objects themselves, underpins the museum’s expansive understanding of design and its relationship to contemporary society. Taking the V&A’s Collections Development Policy as a starting point, this chapter explains its motivations and makes a case for the scope and boundaries of digital collecting within the context of a museum specializing in design. Case studies focusing on two digital objects, the iPhone and WeChat, acquired as part of the museum collection, illustrate how the V&A’s approach to digital collecting brings with it both new opportunities and challenges. These include capturing the ecology of digital design and constructing forms of display and interpretation that consider the social life of an object, its users, and the contexts of its creation and functions. The chapter also looks at some of the challenges that inevitably affect the collection of complex objects, such as ownership, the role of the technology’s user in understanding the design of an object, the place of platforms and corporate intermediaries, and representing distributed experiences. This chapter shares lessons learnt from hands-on curatorial practice, and point to issues and concerns raised in this emerging field of digital collecting, in particular the stewardship and meaningful interpretation of objects in the museum’s care. It concludes with future research agendas and suggested directions. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Simone Natale, Petrina Foti, Ross Parry.

Author: Bonney, Heather E.; Bekvalac, Jelena J.; Phillips, Carina
Title: Human Remains in Museum Collections in the United Kingdom
Abstract: Human remains collections can be found in museums, university departments, and even private collections across the UK. These collections pose many ethical challenges in their management and care, many unique to human remains, which can differ according to the type of holding institution, nature of the collection, and the way in which it is used or studied. These collections are often associated with legacies of poor ethical standards, particularly in terms of early collecting practices. This chapter will explore these factors and the challenges they pose. In the modern context of fluid socio-political and cultural change, museums and other holding institutions are faced with ever-changing external influences and must be able to respond in a dynamic and transparent way. This chapter will also discuss the ethical care and curation of human remains collections in UK museums and other repositories, with a focus on collections acquired and/or curated in England where reference to legislation concerning the care and management of collections is required. Finally, it will explore the concept of harm to communities, public and to science, that can be caused by a lack of transparency and poor decision and policy making with regard to human remains collections. © Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2019, corrected publication 2020.

Author: Tran, Quoc Tan
Title: Situating participation in the backstage: Infrastructural settings impacting museum work
Abstract: This chapter explores the multifaceted dynamics of museum infrastructure extending beyond institutional and departmental boundaries. It addresses the methodological challenges encountered in delving into the backstage operations and practices of the museum staff who meticulously care for objects - the activities that underpin the public-facing practices of object display, engagement, and outreach. The chapter elucidates how an infrastructure studies approach can aid the critical examination of museum work from the perspective of those directly involved in daily operations. Analysing the case of digital transformation at a museum in Berlin, the chapter unveils a complex interplay of tensions, ambiguities, and local adaptations within museum settings. This interplay reflects ongoing negotiations between traditional heritage practices, the contemporary agenda of digital transformation, and the emergence of novel professional roles. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Gertraud Koch and Rachel Charlotte Smith; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Haynes, Rachael
Title: Threads of Resistance: Feminist activism, collaborative making and care ethics
Abstract: This chapter addresses the dual concerns of activism and care ethics through an investigation of collaborative, craft-based strategies in contemporary feminist art practice. Through an intergenerational and intersectional feminist approach, Threads of Resistance reconsiders the relationship between activism and care. The chapter examines how the tactics play out in the space of educational engagement in the contemporary art museum and how the ‘maker space’ offers an inclusive framework for conversations about social justice, voices of difference and an ethics of care. The primary connection between caring and action is also at the heart of ‘ethical caring’: it is the call to take action, to move beyond concern, and to demonstrate and enact care that is vital. For Joan Tronto, to shift the emphasis of daily life in its political, social and economic forms to one focused on care would “transform” our current boundaries, such that the “world will look different.”. © 2022 selection and editorial matter, Jacqueline Millner and Gretchen Coombs; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Morse, Nuala
Title: The museum as a space of social care
Abstract: This book examines the practice of community engagement in museums through the notion of care. It focuses on building an understanding of the logic of care that underpins this practice, with a view to outlining new roles for museums within community health and social care. This book engages with the recent growing focus on community participation in museum activities, notably in the area of health and wellbeing. It explores this theme through an analysis of the practices of community engagement workers at Tyne & Wear Archives & Museums in the UK. It examines how this work is operationalised and valued in the museum, and the institutional barriers to this practice. It presents the practices of care that shape community-led exhibitions, and community engagement projects involving health and social care partners and their clients. Drawing on the ethics of care and geographies of care literatures, this text provides readers with novel perspectives for transforming the museum into a space of social care. This book will appeal to museum studies scholars and professionals, geographers, organisational studies scholars, as well as students interested in the social role of museums. © 2021 Nuala Morse.

Author: Irving, Cat
Title: CONSERVING THE HUMANITY OF HUMAN REMAINS
Abstract: This chapter looks at the history of preservation methods that can be seen in medical museums in Scotland, and the ways conservation work on human remains is essential to the respect necessary to their intrinsic humanity. Human remains in museums have the unique status of being both an object embodying historic and scientific ideas, and actually being the physical vestiges of a person. Conservation work of human remains has to balance a tightrope of care and respect. Where fluid preservation is involved it is possibly less accurate to think of it as conservation in the truest sense, and more a constant maintenance of the conditions suitable to preservation. Rafaela Ferraz described conservation on the head of Portuguese serial killer Diogo Alvez as “Rather than an act of museological preservation, it felt like an act of kindness towards a fellow human being,” which poetically encapsulates this dichotomy. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Trish Biers and Katie Stringer Clary; individual chapters, the contributors.

Title: CARE AS FLOURISHING
Abstract: Care in museums is not a new concept. For many years, museums have talked about “collections care” when it comes to the preservation, conservation, and management of museum objects. Buse et al. expand our notions of “materialities of care” to three interlocking strands, which include spatialities of care, temporalities of care, and practices of care. Contemporary use of empathy involves the capacity to share other people's feelings, to take on others’ perspectives and resonate with how they feel. Museums are uniquely positioned to spark empathy. Self-care is a broad concept that refers to individual responsibility for promoting a healthy lifestyle required for optimal functioning. It involves both the ability to care for oneself and doing the activities necessary to achieve, maintain, or promote optimal health. In a healthy person, self-care is aimed at maintaining physical, psychological, social, and spiritual well-being. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Kiersten F. Latham and Brenda Cowan; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Summers, John
Title: Making Sense of Your Community Museum Collection: Strategies for Stuff Management
Abstract: The chapter gives a comprehensive review of museum collecting concerns as well as the importance of how these are, or should be, managed. Getting collections is the first step in a museum’s stewardship duty. Everything else museums do flows from what is accomplished by this. The author describes the range of problematic collection realities museums often face, especially those devoted to local or regional history. While the various scenarios may seem apocryphal, in fact they are quite honest. They are based on extensive experience improving a range of collection management challenges. Positive outcomes of collection retention stem from how they are acquired. Indeed, one of the most important considerations museums must understand is how they can, or cannot, properly care for potential acquisitions. © 2022 selection and editorial matter, Steven Miller; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Latham, Kiersten F.; Cowan, Brenda
Title: FLOURISHING IN MUSEUMS: Towards a Positive Museology
Abstract: Flourishing in Museums presents the Flourishing Museum Framework, an interdisciplinary model for reflection and practice. Illustrated via a diversity of international examples, the framework demonstrates how museums can meaningfully address the many challenges facing the profession. Including contributions from a wide range of scholar-practitioners working across the arts, humanities, sciences, education, business, and mental health disciplines, the volume uses abundance-thinking and takes a strengths-based appreciative approach to museum purpose, function, and being. The book demonstrates that, even within the most difficult climates, abundance-oriented methods and perspectives can inspire and elicit flourishing in visitors, staff, and communities, thus positioning museums as places where people find meaningful and purposeful work and where visitors find satisfaction, meaning, inspiration, and motivation. Drawing from the disciplines of positive psychology, positive organizational scholarship, contemplative studies, and museum studies, the book is unified and organized into six thematic areas that comprise the Flourishing Museum Framework: courage, transformation, care, optimism, gratitude, and delight. Flourishing in Museums will be essential reading for academics and students working in the museum and heritage fields, as well as the cognate disciplines of arts management and creative industries. It will also be useful to practitioners working in museums and heritage sites around the world. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Kiersten F. Latham and Brenda Cowan; individual chapters, the contributors.

Title: OVERVIEW
Abstract: During the twenty-first century, conservation has become increasingly attuned to the important relationships between individuals, communities, and cultural heritage collections. Partnerships between conservators, communities, and artists have enriched our ability to care for heritage textiles. Many museums and conservators are seeking strategies for the ethical care of captured collections in colonial institutions. Three case studies by Heald; Te Kanawa, Collinge, Blair, and Peranteau; and Stephens demonstrate how conservators can take an active and positive role in ongoing work to foster better relationships between colonial museums and Indigenous communities. Conservators are also called on to care for textiles that come from religious, civic, and military contexts. Three case studies by Rendell, Emery, Scott, and Devenport; van Enckevort, Rumsey, and Gillions; and McLaughlan, Orbell, and Peranteau detail how textile conservators can support community-centred access and preservation. The case study by Barlow provides insight into how conservators can collaborate with contemporary artists and act as informed stewards for their pieces in institutional collections. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Frances Lennard, Patricia Ewer and Laura Mina; individual case studies, the contributors.

Title: INTRODUCTION: The Flourishing Museum Framework
Abstract: The concept of flourishing in museums and the global diversity of illustrative examples provided within this volume use abundance-thinking and a strengths-based appreciative approach to museum purpose, function, and being. Even within the most difficult contexts, abundance-oriented methods and perspectives can inspire and elicit flourishing in visitors, staff, and communities, positioning museums as places where people find meaningful and purposeful work and where visitors find meaning. Museums can enable visitors to flourish across the whole range of topics, when confronted with highly sensitive subjects and challenging perspectives, as well as with lighter fare. Likewise, the synthesis of the tremendous amount of research could help museum workers guide their own practice at work and cultivate a culture of care in museum work. Recognizing museums as complex, dynamic systems allows us insight into the connections and causes for why things exist as they do and gives us the power to make choices that lead to change. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Kiersten F. Latham and Brenda Cowan; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Zimmermann, Corinne
Title: CULTIVATING COMPASSION IN THE MUSEUM WORKPLACE
Abstract: Often invisible to audiences, it is the museum staff who keep museums running and functioning smoothly. Yet, much focus and effort go into creating successful visitor experiences. In order to enable flourishing in visitors, museums need to enable it in their employees. In this chapter, Zimmerman addresses the care of museum staff and the need for creating a psychologically safe environment, providing practical strategies for cultivating a healthy workplace. With methods from her work with healthcare teams, she offers insights and designs for creativity, connection, compassion, and resilience in museum workers and teams. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Kiersten F. Latham and Brenda Cowan; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Guidess, Gretchen
Title: TO REVEAL AND NOT OBSCURE: Balancing conservation and visual access
Abstract: The collections of The Colonial Williamsburg Foundation play a vital role in serving its educational mission. In addition to being displayed in regularly changing exhibitions in one of three dedicated textile galleries in the Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Folk Art Museum and the DeWitt Wallace Decorative Arts Museum, the collection of historic garments and textiles is routinely examined by Foundation staff. Curators, historic tradespeople and the team that creates wardrobes for costumed interpreters all use the collection to inform their work. The collection is also available to and regularly accessed by visiting scholars and students. This frequent access to the collection for rigorous scholarship shapes all preservation decisions, from methods of storage to treatment intervention. Textile conservation staff regularly confer with these groups of dedicated stakeholders to devise conservation treatments that serve the long-term preservation goals of collection’s care while providing the visual access required for the study and deeper understanding of the collection. This has resulted in a range of storage methods, display mounts and a body of priorities and considerations that guide treatment of the collection. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Frances Lennard, Patricia Ewer and Laura Mina; individual case studies, the contributors.

Author: Brown, Steve
Title: FORGIVENESS: In Conversation With 3,397 Indigenous Stone Tools
Abstract: Can objects forgive? Do museums and heritage sites have a right to ask Indigenous objects for their forgiveness? Why does repatriation of Indigenous objects focus on human remains and “secret/sacred” objects and not on those considered mundane or every day? And how can museological repatriation practices become enactments of care, respect, and mutual engagement? This piece will focus on the over 3,397 Indigenous stone tools that were collected (“salvaged”) for the Western Australian Museum over 44 years ago, and Steve Brown’s process of seeking their forgiveness for having been removed from the traditional country (or territories) of their Indigenous custodians. This piece will share methods in auto-ethnography, auto-hermeneutics, phenomenology, videography, contemplation, and practices linked to affect and emotion studies, to extend ideas of “return” to all Indigenous objects, especially those typically categorized as “archaeological.” The collection of stone tools will be explored as facilitators and mediators of “soft diplomacy” and human encounter, to enable conversations/dialogs between museums and Indigenous owners/custodians which can support the building of civil societies, including communities of peoples and objects. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Kiersten F. Latham and Brenda Cowan; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Silence, Patricia
Title: PREVENTIVE CONSERVATION AT THE COLONIAL WILLIAMSBURG FOUNDATION
Abstract: The Colonial Williamsburg Foundation implements a comprehensive preventive conservation programme to care for its diverse collections, including textiles found in archaeological, historical, fine art, and architectural categories. The programme involves collaboration among departments and trades within the institution, and addresses catastrophic risks, environmental damage, and routine collection maintenance. While antique textiles are rarely displayed due to their vulnerability, high-quality reproduction textiles are showcased throughout the Historic Area. The preventive conservation team, consisting of local employees with diverse skills, inspects, cleans, and gathers data on a daily basis. The programme emphasizes the long-term benefits of preventive conservation, preserving cultural heritage material for future generations. Disaster preparedness plans cover both natural and man-made disasters, with staff training and emergency supplies in place. Fire detection and suppression systems are carefully evaluated and maintained. The role of preventive conservators extends to building and mechanical systems design, lighting management, pest prevention, and integrated pest management. Technology and data analysis enhance the effectiveness of preventive conservation practices. In conclusion, the paper emphasizes the significance of preventive conservation in preserving textile collections and the need for collaboration, communication, and technological tools to achieve optimal collections care. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Frances Lennard, Patricia Ewer and Laura Mina; individual case studies, the contributors.

Author: Rasmussen, Briley A.; DiCindio, Carissa
Title: Gathering Online: A Collaborative Project with Graduate Museum Education Students During COVID-19
Abstract: This chapter discusses a project designed by two faculty in their art museum education courses respectively at the University of Texas at Austin and the University of Arizona requiring students from the two institutions to collaborate with one another and develop asynchronous virtual tours exploring collections on both campuses. Prior to the pandemic, each course included a project in which students developed in-person facilitated gallery experiences at a university art museum or gallery. These projects were adapted to create a single project across universities utilising online programmes and tools to collaborate virtually. Through this project, students considered how art museums can serve as sites for intentional gatherings through asynchronous digital experiences that focus on community and connection. They engaged with their university art museums through experiential learning opportunities focused on connection, health, and care. Finally, they examined how cross-university partnerships can build opportunities for peer learning, collaboration, and experimentation through new perspectives and voices. Through this collaboration, students engaged in participatory practices and multimodal learning opportunities; they gained multiple perspectives into gallery teaching and professional experience that they can take with them in the field. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Leda Cempellin and Pat Crawford; individual chapters, the contributors. All rights reserved.

Author: Howard, Sarah
Title: WORKING WITH SYNTHETIC FIBRES: The response of textile conservation to twentieth-century dress
Abstract: The introduction of synthetic fibres in the twentieth century, and their increasing use across the century for the manufacture of items of dress and accessories, create a diverse range of issues for their ongoing care and preservation. Increased awareness and understanding of the significance of the everyday, not just the couture, has increased the demand to view twentieth-century collections. Approaches to the conservation of such materials has led to an increasing bank of knowledge and experience, and scientific support has helped to understand the often complex array of synthetic materials that respond differently to the environment in which they are displayed and stored. This article offers a pragmatic approach to the preservation of synthetic materials, reviewing some of the most recent advances in scientific research and experiences gained to highlight the problems facing textile conservators today. Using a case study of storage in an independent museum to proffer solutions, the article examines preventive conservation measures and analyses their effectiveness in preserving twentieth-century synthetic materials. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Frances Lennard, Patricia Ewer and Laura Mina; individual case studies, the contributors.

Author: Keefe, Anna Rose; Irvin, Kate; Urick, Jessica
Title: INHERENT VICE, OR: How I learned to stop worrying and love shattered silk
Abstract: This case study describes a year-long project, ‘Inherent Vice’, at the Rhode Island School of Design (RISD) Museum, which engaged student artists with conservation and collections care work. As part of this initiative, conceived by conservators and curators in consultation with local artists and the RISD community, deaccessioned garments from the Museum’s collection were provided to students for creative exploration and reuse. These Gilded Age garments - featuring severe damage such as shattered silk, desiccated thread and other examples of inherent vice - became the basis for dialogue and reflection and were transformed into new works of art that interrogate historical legacy and missing narratives within museums. This case study summarizes the internal planning, community conversations, academic courses, and two exhibitions developed from this project. It argues that conservation thinking is a valuable addition to creative practice and that conservators should not view deterioration as a failure but rather as a jumping-off point where new ideas, new works, and new relationships can thrive. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Frances Lennard, Patricia Ewer and Laura Mina; individual case studies, the contributors.

Author: Brennan, Julia M.
Title: TEACHING PREVENTIVE CONSERVATION AND TEXTILE TREATMENTS IN ASIA AND AFRICA
Abstract: Conservation training in global communities is about partnerships, identifying sustainable and local skills and materials, and above all respecting the cultural owners. While the cultures, climates, languages, material artefacts and institutions vary, the goals and needs are the same - to train in practical preventive care and textile conservation practices, build staff capacity, improve the methods and conditions for protecting cultural heritage and stimulate national policies for preservation. Working in situ and in collaboration with the stewards of culture has lifelong impacts; it fosters ongoing professional relationships, creative solutions to challenging problems and a flourishing exchange of knowledge and methods. Drawn from case studies in Bhutan, Algeria, Cambodia, Thailand and Laos, this case study proposes an approach for teaching both theories and practices that honour culture, religion and geography in order to creatively develop localized conservation solutions, while deepening skill sets and personal specializations. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Frances Lennard, Patricia Ewer and Laura Mina; individual case studies, the contributors.

Author: Hughes, Helen M.
Title: INSTITUTIONAL DEVELOPMENTS AND THEIR EFFECT ON CONSERVATION POLICIES: The Cambusnethan Bog Burial Coat
Abstract: This case history begins by looking at organizational developments in Glasgow Museums that have affected the role of the author as a textile conservator. The main body of the case history focuses on a coat worn by the man whose body was found in the Cambusnethan bog at Greenhead Moss. There is an account of the discovery of the body, early research and analysis of the body and clothing, past treatments and the author’s involvement with the coat. Sections on human remains and repatriation demonstrate Glasgow Museums’ responses to societal changes where there is a greater awareness and emotional concern for the care of human remains. The concluding discussion illustrates changes to the author’s role in relation to the coat, showing how communication and public engagement are increasingly important for a conservator, and the impact on decisions and thoughts about the future treatment and care of the coat. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Frances Lennard, Patricia Ewer and Laura Mina; individual case studies, the contributors.

Author: McLaughlan, Fiona; Orbell, Claire; Peranteau, Anne
Title: THE SCOTS COLOURS AT TOITU OTAGO SETTLERS MUSEUM: Use, preservation and protocol
Abstract: This paper explores the transfer of two Regimental flags, known as the ‘Scots Colours’, to the Toitu Otago Settlers Museum (TOSM) in New Zealand. The museum, founded in 1898, focuses on the history and heritage of Dunedin and the Otago region. The New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) loaned the flags for long-term preservation. The event of laying up the flags at TOSM was celebrated with a parade and attended by dignitaries. The preservation and care of the flags involve adherence to NZDF protocols and museological practices. The flags are displayed annually for two weeks around Anzac Day, attracting numerous visitors. The museum ensures their protection while making them visible through elevated displays. Specific conditions, including consultation with the NZDF for public display and conservation treatment, are part of the loan agreement. The flags, pikes, and finials are stored separately in custom-made boxes and undergo regular monitoring and condition reporting. Access to the flags is facilitated for NZDF personnel, researchers, and the public, fostering a connection with former members of the NZ Scottish Regiment. Overall, the paper discusses the significance of the Scots Colours, their preservation at TOSM, the conservation treatment undertaken, and the collaboration between the museum and the NZDF in safeguarding these historical artefacts. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Frances Lennard, Patricia Ewer and Laura Mina; individual case studies, the contributors.

Author: Colomer, Laia Domingo; Schmitt, Edwin
Title: MAPPING MEMORIALISATION OF PANDEMIC EXPERIENCES: Care, stewardship and guardianship
Abstract: Many spontaneous memorials emerged worldwide after COVID-19, followed by national and local authorities organising official periods of public mourning. In the scholarly context of memory studies, these rituals are framed as memorialisation processes. Between October and December 2020, we systematically mapped these memorials and categorised them into ceremonies, monuments, cybermemorials or public protests. This chapter introduces this mapping as an example of the cultural heritage of trauma and further explores its impact on social well-being and political dimensions. This exercise is to be understood as the seed for future scholarly research on the memorialisation of the COVID-19 pandemic, a material guide for museum curators collecting on coronavirus impacts or a database for any exhibition on the topic. Drawing on the ethics of care, we have finally reflected on the ethics embedded in all these unfolding processes, from the occurrence of the mourning rituals to the fact that some of these expressions of loss and grief might finally be transformed into the cultural heritage of COVID-19 pandemic trauma. © 2024 selection and editorial matter, Alexandra Bounia and Andrea Witcomb; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Chitty, Gill
Title: Heritage, conservation and communities: Engagement, participation and capacity building
Abstract: Public participation and local community involvement have taken centre stage in heritage practice in recent decades. In contrast with this established position in wider heritage work, public engagement with conservation practice is less well developed. The focus here is on conservation as the practical care of material cultural heritage, with all its associated significance for local people. How can we be more successful in building capacity for local ownership and leadership of heritage conservation projects, as well as improving participative involvement in decisions and in practice? This book presents current research and practice in community-led conservation. It illustrates that outcomes of locally-led, active participation show demonstrable social, educational and personal benefits for participants. Bringing together UK and international case studies, the book combines analysis of theoretical and applied approaches, exploring the lived experiences of conservation projects in and with different communities. Responding to the need for deeper understanding of the outcomes of heritage conservation, it examines the engagement of local people and communities beyond the expert and specialist domain. Highlighting the advances in this important aspect of contemporary heritage practice, this book is a key resource for practitioners in heritage studies, conservation and heritage management. It is also relevant for the practising professional, student or university researcher in an emerging field that overarches professional and academic practice. © 2017 selection and editorial matter, Gill Chitty.

Title: Well-Being and Art Museums
Abstract: This chapter examines how art museums are evolving to address well-being among youth through two case studies from Asia. The Yokohama Museum of Art in Japan presents a unique program targeting hikikomori youth-young people experiencing extreme social withdrawal. Through various art activities, the museum created safe and welcoming spaces that helped these individuals gradually rebuild their self-confidence and social connections. The second case study from National Gallery Singapore details the pilot of a six-session Strength Through Art (stART) program designed to foster emotional resilience among 12-15 year-old students. Both cases also demonstrate how art museums can partner with various stakeholders to support the mental well-being of young people. The chapter concludes with broader discussions of how art museums can serve as spaces of care for youth audiences. It examines how museums' unique environments and audience-centered approaches provide much-needed avenues for youth to engage in looking at art, talking about art and making art in ways that support self-awareness and emotional regulation, encourage shared understanding and social connection. Together, these perspectives illuminate how art museums can expand their roles as active partners in nurturing the emotional and psychological well-being of the next generation. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, Heather Maxson, Susan McCullough, and Ai Wee Seow; individual chapters, the contributors. All rights reserved.
Manual Tags: Art museums; Museums; Well being; Young peoples; Case-studies; National Gallery; Program targeting; Self awareness; Shared understanding; Singapore; Social behavior; Social connection

Author: Forsko, Samantha
Title: Practical Approaches to Collections Care
Abstract: While cultural heritage practitioners and caretakers are often intimidated by "best practices," Practical Approaches to Collections Care helps to alleviate those concerns, offering a stepped approach to preservation encompassing a variety of collections care programs. The author, drawing on over a decade of experience working in libraries, museums, archives, and other historic sites, and specifically building off of her work as a Preservation Specialist at the Conservation Center for Art & Historic Artifacts, discusses realistic, efficient, and sustainable approaches to collection housing, space planning, environmental management, facilities care, emergency preparedness, and much more. Giving examples of implementation and easy-to-follow guides that will allow readers to start from scratch or improve an already existing program, Forsko demonstrates how preservation can become a component of any collections care program. Encouraging the reader to start by taking small, manageable steps, the author shows that even the smallest of actions can make a difference that will ultimately help to preserve collections and ensure that the world’s heritage will remain intact for future generations. Practical Approaches to Collections Care takes an applied approach, making suggestions the reader can immediately implement no matter the size of their institution. It is an essential tool for stewards of cultural heritage collections, particularly collections managers, registrars, and preservation specialists. It will also be useful to students who are engaged in the study of collections care. © 2023 Samantha Forsko. All rights reserved.

Author: Colomer, Laia Domingo; González-Marcén, Paloma; Picazo, Marina Ferreras
Title: FEMINIST ARCHAEOLOGY FOR THE PRESENT: Maintenance activities and social caring
Abstract: This chapter introduces the notion of maintenance activities as an epistemological category that frames our approach to applied research as a feminist practice when exploring the past from and for the present. Drawing on the feminist political movement, we understand archaeology as a practice that develops forms of engendering research, practice, and behaviours in academic milieus. It also formulates new knowledge of the past that contributes towards changing patriarchal visions of the present through its implementation in education and heritage milieus by the Pastwomen network. Furthermore, this chapter incorporates the ethics of care as an ontological and epistemological notion that helps to better frame and complement the notion of maintenance activities. To illustrate this, some examples are provided from our research work in the fields of archaeology, heritage studies, and specifically, the dissemination project carried out by the Pastwomen network. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Marianne Moen and Unn Pedersen; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Dekker, Annet; Archey, Karen; Blair, Ulanda; Cook, Sarah; Magalhães, Ana Gonçalves; Himmelsbach, Sabine; Nichole, Kelani; Paul, Christiane; Paunu, Henna
Title: A ROUNDTABLE: CURATORIAL PERSPECTIVES ON COLLECTING TIME-BASED MEDIA ART
Abstract: This chapter focuses on how curators are becoming more closely connected and involved in preservation practice, particularly when it involves time-based media artworks. While this happens at various stages, from production to exhibition and collecting, the conversation was aimed at the acquisition process and collection practice of time-based media art. The chapter presents a summary of the discussion focusing on some of the key commonalities, such as the need for technical and curatorial knowledge, the usefulness and obstructions of standardization, the benefits of collaboration, and the potentialities of shared and distributed networks of knowledge and care. The diversity of documentation strategies emphasizes how time-based media is changing the museum practice in which the traditional functions of curator and conservator are shifting, as the care of an artwork is not only about repairing or even envisioning future change, but also about following and documenting its evolving “collection life”. © 2023 selection and editorial matter, Deena Engel and Joanna Phillips; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Pegno, Marianna; Souffrant, Kantara
Title: Institutional Change for Museums: A Practical Guide to Creating Polyvocal Spaces
Abstract: Institutional Change for Museums: A Practical Guide to Creating Polyvocal Spaces is an edited volume borne of two questions: (1) What do we want from museums? (2) Why do we (still) care to fight for these visions? Rooted in the concept of polyvocality—the blending of multiple perspectives, experiences, and ideas, where differences and conflicting truths are welcome—this co-written introduction explores these questions and the future potential of museums. The authors begin with their personal “museum journeys.” Representing individuals who grew up going to museums and those who stepped into museums later in life, the journeys challenge singular, universal, homogenous museum practice. The narratives reflect the burgeoning potentials of museums and the authors’ complicated experiences with these institutions while modeling a polyvocal practice and mirror the book’s tone: one that honors multiple truths in various written styles. Following the museum journeys is a theoretical review of polyvocality. The introduction concludes by summarizing the three sections in the volume: Part I, “Interrogating and Redressing Colonial Legacies”; Part II, “Rethinking Structures and Operations”; and Part III, “Agency and Ethics of Care.” Collectively, these sections argue for polyvocality as a necessary concept vital to the future of museums. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Marianna Pegno and Kantara Souffrant; individual chapters, the contributors.
Manual Tags: Museums; Blending; Institutional change; Multiple perspectives; Practical guide

Author: Jarczyk, Agathe; Oleksik, Peter
Title: CARING FOR ANALOG AND DIGITAL VIDEO ART
Abstract: Video artworks comprise the majority of time-based media artworks in museum collections due to the long and rich history of artists engaging with this medium. This chapter explores the history of video as an artistic medium, gives a short insight on collecting practices, and offers practical advice on the long-term care of this volatile material in a collection. Collection care of time-based media artworks is an ongoing process with a number of important key moments. Acquisition and intake lay the groundwork for creating comprehensive documentation on the concept, production, and display of video artworks. Automated critical viewing is possible with software tools that analyze the video and audio stream and flag certain elements that it has been configured to identify. In the process of digitization, time base correctors (TBCs) are usually required for all analog formats to stabilize the analog signal. A TBC buffers the unstable input analog signal and sends out a stabilized analog signal as a result. © 2023 selection and editorial matter, Deena Engel and Joanna Phillips; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Kramer, Lia; Nichols, Alexandra; Anderson, Mollie; Kennedy, Nora W.; López, Lorena Ramírez; Wharton, Glenn
Title: INSTITUTIONAL ASSESSMENTS AND COLLECTION SURVEYS FOR TIME-BASED MEDIA CONSERVATION
Abstract: This chapter deals with traditional methods developed for cultural heritage institutions and how they can be adapted to serve the unique needs of time-based media (TBM) collections. It then provide guidelines for planning and executing institutional assessments and collection surveys, along with implementing recommendations in the final report. A TBM institutional assessment guides an organization toward developing strategies for improved care and display of TBM artworks. The assessment helps staff focus efforts on the immediate needs of the collection, such as obtaining master-quality files or backing up artist-provided materials, as well as achieve longer-term goals, such as establishing permanent staff positions, creating a TBM conservation lab, or building a digital repository. A registration and cataloging review for TBM artworks verifies that the institution owns all the components that are necessary to preserve and display the works and that these components are consistently cataloged in the institution’s collection management system and tracked with locations. © 2023 selection and editorial matter, Deena Engel and Joanna Phillips; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Pegno, Marianna; Souffrant, Kantara
Title: Introduction
Abstract: Institutional Change for Museums: A Practical Guide to Creating Polyvocal Spaces is an edited volume borne of two questions: (1) What do we want from museums? (2) Why do we (still) care to fight for these visions? Rooted in the concept of polyvocality—the blending of multiple perspectives, experiences, and ideas, where differences and conflicting truths are welcome—this co-written introduction explores these questions and the future potential of museums. The authors begin with their personal “museum journeys.” Representing individuals who grew up going to museums and those who stepped into museums later in life, the journeys challenge singular, universal, homogenous museum practice. The narratives reflect the burgeoning potentials of museums and the authors’ complicated experiences with these institutions while modeling a polyvocal practice and mirror the book’s tone: one that honors multiple truths in various written styles. Following the museum journeys is a theoretical review of polyvocality. The introduction concludes by summarizing the three sections in the volume: Part I, “Interrogating and Redressing Colonial Legacies”; Part II, “Rethinking Structures and Operations”; and Part III, “Agency and Ethics of Care.” Collectively, these sections argue for polyvocality as a necessary concept vital to the future of museums. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Marianna Pegno and Kantara Souffrant; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Martin, Nicole
Title: DIGITAL PRESERVATION AND THE INFORMATION PACKAGE
Abstract: This chapter introduces digital preservation standards and practices established in the libraries and archives community and presents their relevance to the care of audiovisual heritage and time-based media art collections. Collection stewards begin the process of digital preservation by investigating the past or history of data in their possession, documenting that information to make certain it is available to future users indefinitely. This background information creates context and makes data more meaningful, helping future users understand how a file was created, how it was used, and who used it. Preservationists also document information about the file in its present state. The Open Archival Information Systems (OAIS) model has a “particular focus on digital information,” both in terms of the data contained in a package and method of description, but is not restricted to the virtual world and can be applied to physical collections, as well. © 2023 selection and editorial matter, Deena Engel and Joanna Phillips; individual chapters, the contributors.

Author: Marcus, Uncle; Clark, Lucy; Gissell, Tammi; Sentance, Nathan
Title: INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGES IN POWERHOUSE CUSTODIANSHIP: Building Trust, Building Collections
Abstract: The Deed of Deposit is a pioneering mechanism developed by the Powerhouse Museum. It redefines the relationship between Indigenous communities and collecting institutions by preserving Indigenous ownership of cultural knowledge while enabling museum care and stewardship. Rooted in the post-custodial approach, the Deed challenges entrenched colonial collecting practices and responds to the ethical concerns outlined by the Indigenous Archives Collective. Traditional museum and archive collections have often excluded Indigenous consent, fostering deep mistrust. The Deed of Deposit, however, ensures that Indigenous sovereignty and self-determination are upheld by keeping ownership with rightful custodians rather than transferring it to institutions. This chapter explores the development, implementation, and implications of the Deed from both cultural and practical standpoints, illustrating how it serves as a decolonial model for ethical collecting. By positioning institutions as facilitators, not owners, the Powerhouse is reshaping its role in cultural heritage management. Looking ahead, sustained collaboration, advocacy, and policy development will be essential in ensuring that the Deed continues to honour Indigenous rights and transform museum practice. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, The Indigenous Archives Collective; individual chapters, the contributors.
